$ALLO : The Lifeblood of Allora’s Intelligent Economy @AlloraNetwork is building something powerful — a decentralized system where anyone can request predictions, contribute AI models, and improve outcomes over time. At the center of this system is the $ALLO. It’s not just a cryptocurrency. It’s the fuel that keeps the network running, growing, and learning. let’s break down how ALLO is used, in the simplest way possible. 🔧 1. You Choose the Price: Pay-What-You-Want Allora does something very different. When you ask the network for a prediction (called an “inference”), you choose how much you want to pay using ALLO tokens. This model is called Pay-What-You-Want (PWYW). How it works: -If you pay more ALLO → your request gets more attention, and contributors are rewarded. -If you pay nothing → the topic becomes inactive over time, and no one earns rewards from it. This keeps the network fair and demand-driven. You’re not forced to pay a fixed price — instead, you pay based on how valuable the answer is to you. 🧪 2. Creating and Joining Topics Allora is organized into topics. Each topic is a specific area where predictions are made — like “Bitcoin price in 5 minutes” or “Ethereum gas fees tomorrow.” To participate in a topic, whether as: a Worker (someone who submits predictions), or a Reputer (someone who scores predictions), …you need to pay a small fee in ALLO to register. This helps filter out spam and makes sure only serious participants join. It also gives the topic weight, which affects how much reward it can attract. 🔐 3. Staking & Delegation: Earn by Supporting the Network ALLO is also used for staking — which means locking up tokens to support the network and earn rewards. Here’s how it works: -Reputers stake ALLO to prove they are trustworthy. -Validators stake ALLO to help secure the network. -Regular users can delegate their ALLO to a reputer or validator and earn a share of the rewards. Staking creates trust and accountability. The more ALLO someone has at stake, the more careful they are about doing quality work. 🎁 4. Earning Rewards in ALLO Everyone who helps the network gets paid in ALLO: -Workers earn when their predictions are accurate. -Reputers earn for giving fair scores. -Validators earn for maintaining honest consensus. -Delegators earn a portion of the rewards from the people they support. Where do these rewards come from? -A portion comes from inference payments (PWYW). -The rest comes from newly released ALLO tokens through emissions. 📉 5. Emissions and Long-Term Value ALLO tokens are released over time in a schedule similar to Bitcoin’s halving model. This means: -Fewer new tokens are released as time goes on. -Early participants are rewarded more. -The supply is limited and predictable. Allora also makes sure that rewards stay stable, even when tokens unlock. This prevents big price drops and encourages people to stake long-term instead of selling quickly. ALLO is More Than Just a Token ALLO is what keeps the @AlloraNetwork alive and evolving. It’s how users show what they value. It’s how contributors are paid fairly. It’s how reputation, trust, and incentives stay aligned.

With the early presidential election and the launch of a new government, all we can do now is hope for better governance. In line with the new administration, I’m reviewing and adjusting my portfolio and taking stock of the asset markets. The new government has signaled aggressive fiscal expansion, promising large-scale support for small businesses and household livelihoods. Programs like the nationwide 250,000 KRW “Livelihood Recovery Payment” and support for Itaewon disaster victims have already been announced, with a supplementary budget also expected. With more money flowing into the economy, a decline in the value of the Korean won seems likely. That’s why I plan to maintain my allocation to dollar-denominated assets. Between US stocks and Bitcoin, Bitcoin actually looks more promising, given the likely sideways movement in US equities. Real estate polarization will likely accelerate. Prime residential properties in Seoul will become even more attractive, while a rebound in commercial or regional real estate seems unlikely. If Korea follows Japan’s path, owning a single high-quality residential property in a prime location will be essential. Considering the property price surge under the previous progressive government, those “one solid home” assets could become unaffordable in a few years. Of course, real estate policy is a key variable, so I’ll be keeping an eye on that. Personally, I don’t see clear new growth engines for Korea’s future economy. Despite ambitions to become a top-three AI powerhouse, the reality looks tough. Our main industries—semiconductors, autos, shipbuilding—are already being caught up by China and other competitors. With working hours set to decrease further, productivity gains will be hard to achieve. Still, stock markets don’t always move in lockstep with the real economy. Whether we see KOSPI 5000 or not, the government is likely to roll out more capital market reforms and stock-boosting measures. With ample liquidity and a rising real estate market, I think many people will continue to see “wealth accumulation through domestic stocks → real estate purchase” as the path forward, so Korean equities could still rise. GhostDAG, a proof-of-work consensus protocol that generalizes Nakamoto’s chain into a directed acyclic graph of blocks ( blockDAG). GhostDAG incorporates”orphan” blocks into the chain to form a blockDAG, and then uses a novel greedy algorithm to order the blocks such that well-connected, honest blocks are favored, quickly and with high probability. GhostDAG allows Kaspa to circumvent the traditional tradeoff of blockchains, improving on block rate by orders of magnitude while maintaining the theoretical security guarantees of Bitcoin. The DAGKNIGHT Protocol, written by Michael Sutton and Yonatan Sompolinsky, is a three-year work of genius and consensus upgrade for Kaspa’s PHANTOM GHOSTDAG Protocol. KNIGHT was set in motion with the goal of resisting 50% attacks without knowing the network latency ahead of time. Typically, blockchain protocols assume a parameter of network delay for best and/or worst-case scenarios without the ability to adapt to real-time latency. This assumed latency parameter keeps blockchains restrained to slower confirmation times to avoid security risks and instability. A 50% or 51% attack occurs when a group or entity owns more than 50% of the nodes on the network, granting the controlling parties the ability to alter the blockchain. However, with network delay left unaddressed, if latency spikes, the percentage of ownership needed for an attack decreases. Subsequently leaving the chain more susceptible to an attack. To fix this, blockchains sacrifice block confirmation time to account for the ailing network health by setting an estimated/assumed network delay parameter.
